reading.rtitle: What a Buyer Sees When They Walk Your Plant
paras: Every large retailer sends somebody to look at a supplier before the first big order, and almost every supplier prepares for the wrong visit. The plant gets cleaned, the newest machine is running, and the best operator is on the line. None of that is what the visitor came for. A buyer walking a plant is trying to answer one question, and it is not whether you can make the product. It is whether you can make it again next February, on the day it is needed, when something has gone wrong.

So the visitor looks at the parts of the floor nobody puts in the brochure. Roughly how much scrap is sitting at the end of the line, and is somebody counting it. Where the bottleneck is, and whether the people working there know it is the bottleneck. How long the changeover between two batches takes, because that number, more than capacity, decides how small an order you can accept without losing money. And, quietly, how many people are on the floor compared with the headcount on the paperwork.

Auditors who do this for a living tend to say the same two things. First, that a plant running at ninety per cent of capacity is a warning, not an achievement, because there is nothing left for the week when a machine goes down. Second, that the best answer a supplier can give to a difficult question is a number and a date. In the region of forty thousand units a week, give or take, and we have not missed a delivery date since March. Precision, not polish, is what gets a supplier through the visit.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: We produce in the region of forty thousand units a week.
Capacity is around sixty thousand, so we run at roughly two thirds.
Downtime last year was just under two per cent of scheduled hours.
Scrap is well below three per cent, and we weigh it every shift.
A changeover between batches takes forty minutes, give or take.
Headcount is a hundred and twenty, plus a good deal more in high season.

listenings.text: Let me give you the week rather than the year, because the year always sounds better than it is. We ran five days and a Saturday morning. Output was in the region of thirty-eight thousand units, which is a little under where we should be, and I know exactly why. We lost most of Tuesday afternoon to downtime on the second line, roughly four hours, and a changeover on Thursday took nearly an hour longer than it should have because the batch before it had a scrap problem we did not catch early enough. Take those two out and we would have been at forty-one, forty-two thousand, give or take. Capacity, if you want the honest number, is somewhere around fifty-five thousand a week, but nobody should ever run at fifty-five thousand. You need the room.

People assume I arrive with a checklist and tick boxes for two hours, and I do have a checklist, but it is not what tells me anything. What tells me things is what the floor does when nobody has been warned. I want to see where the slowest point in the process is, and I want to see whether the two people standing at it know that it is the slowest point, because if they do, somebody has told them, and that means somebody is managing the line rather than just running it. I look at the scrap. Not how much there is, particularly, but whether anybody is counting it, and whether the number they give me matches what I can see. And I always ask the same last question, which is what went wrong most recently and what happened afterwards. Plenty of suppliers tell me nothing has gone wrong, and that is the answer I trust the least.
